# The Keeper of Glass

The lighthouse at Corran Point had stood for a hundred and twelve years, and for the last thirty of them it had been kept by a woman named Maren Ostby, who did not like visitors and rarely got any. The island was a knuckle of black rock a mile off the coast, reachable only when the tide allowed the causeway to surface, and in November it almost never did.

Maren kept the lamp lit each night, wound the clockwork that turned the great lens, logged the weather in a ledger with a cracked green cover, and climbed the spiral stairs every dawn to polish the brass. The work was exacting and it was lonely, and she had made her peace with both. What she had not made peace with was the sea's habit of giving back things it had taken.

The first piece of glass she found was on the eastern shelf, wedged between two boulders where the swell pushed kelp into long brown ropes. It was the size of a thumbnail, frosted white on every face, with a faint blue core like a bruise healing. She held it up to the gray noon light and thought of nothing at all for almost a full minute, which was unusual for her.

That was the beginning of the collection.

She kept it in a tin that had once held peppermints, lined with a square of grey wool. At first there were only a few pieces: a green so pale it looked like new leaves, a brown the colour of strong tea, one stubborn white that had survived what must have been decades of grinding. Then the pieces multiplied. The sea, it turned out, was a patient manufacturer. Bottles broke on the rocks. Jars went over the side from passing boats. Some old glassworks, long closed, had dumped its cullet somewhere up the coast, and the tides had been sorting it ever since, rolling each shard against the next until the edges softened into something like fog.

Maren learned to read the beaches the way other people read faces. Glass collected in the lee of the big boulder at low spring tide. The best blues came after storms that churned the shingle, when the sea had been busy and careless. Sunlight through a piece of cobalt sea glass could throw a small, trembling oval of colour onto the whitewashed wall of the keeper's room, and in the afternoons she would sit with her tea and watch it move across the plaster as the light shifted.

She did not tell anyone about the collection. The supply boat came twice a month, and its skipper, a talkative man named Haddow, would have made a joke of it, or worse, a fuss. Maren preferred the glass to remain hers, a private inventory, like a ledger of quiet days.

But one winter, a letter arrived from the Lighthouse Board in the city. The island was to be automated. The lens would be replaced by a electric beacon on a steel mast, and the keeper's position would be discontinued at the end of the year. There would be a pension, the letter said, and a placement assistance programme. Maren read it twice, folded it into quarters, and put it in the drawer beneath the logbook.

She did not sleep much that week. She climbed the stairs every night and sat with the lamp turning above her, the great lens throwing its slow beam across the water, and she thought about the rock and the glass and the thousand small things the sea had made and then unmade and then made again.

On the last Sunday of the month, the tide was low and the causeway lay bare under a thin sun. Maren walked out to the eastern shelf with the peppermint tin under her arm. The wind was cold and the kelp smelled of iodine and rot. She knelt on the wet stones, opened the tin, and began to sort.

It took her the whole afternoon. She laid the pieces out in rows on a flat slab of granite, the way she imagined a jeweller might, grouping them by colour and then by size. The whites in one line, the greens in another, the browns and ambers in a third, and at the end, the blues, which she had always thought were the finest of all. There were more of them than she had realised. Sixty-one in total, not counting the broken ones she had kept out of sentiment.

When the light began to slant toward evening, she gathered them back into the tin one row at a time. Then, instead of carrying it up to the keeper's room, she walked down the shingle to the water's edge and poured the glass into the shallows, slowly, a little at a time, so that the pieces slid and clicked against each other as they went under.

The sea took them without ceremony. Within a minute they were indistinguishable from the stones around them.

Maren stood there until the cold got into her boots. Then she walked back up the causeway, climbed the stairs, and lit the lamp a little early, because the sky over the water had turned the colour of bruised plums and the ships would be coming in.

She kept the logbook that night, as she always did. Under the weather and the visibility and the tide, she wrote a single line: *Left a collection to the sea. It has better hands for it.*

The new beacon would be installed in the spring. Until then, the old lens turned, its light sweeping the dark water, and Maren Ostby kept watch over the rock that had given her the only treasures she had ever wanted, and that would, when the time came, let her go without a word.
